story_text.value:
Hey HN,

I find myself in this situation almost daily:

- I have some long-running task in my session going - I queue up a few more prompts as that task is running, in the same session. - I realize I want to to edit, re-order, delete or consolidate one of those several queued prompts

I'm surprised to not find intuitive and seamless support for this workflow. I use github copilot CLI as my daily driver (MSFT employee), but I have tried claude code, opencode and other harnesses as well. I realize I could start another /session , but often times the queued prompts build upon eachother or the currently running task, so it makes more sense to be able to edit them and wait for the current work to be done.

I'm imagining a /queue command that brings up a TUI list of the queued prompts, or perhaps a vim window with all of them and you can edit them in a similar way to how you do "git rebase -i" and pick/squash git commits if that makes sense.

Perhaps some of the more GUI harnesses have better queue management.

How are you handling this scenario?

Thanks, Happy thanksgiving!

title.value: Ask HN: Do coding harnesses not have prompt queue management features?

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Nathan. I wanted to share a project that I've been working on this month.

A few weeks ago, my Rust target folders had grown to about 70 GB across many git worktrees, and I asked Claude to figure out how to stop that from happening. It couldn't find much online, so we started to build our own workaround using some unstable cargo flags. Then someone on r/rust asked why we hadn't just used kache. Someone else mentioned Mr Boxington on a GitHub issue (another great solution).

I also got annoyed that my Claude Code sessions would constantly ask me to reauthenticate my MCP servers, which happens when you run a lot of them in parallel. An agent couldn't find any good "MCP proxy" so we started planning and building our own. I searched Google myself and found MCPProxy.app. It worked pretty well so I wrote a blog post and shared it on X. Some people replied and told me that Executor.sh was an even better solution. They were right, so I switched to Executor.

After all this, I decided to build Talira: A search engine for software that an AI agent can check before it starts building your own solution. You describe the problem in plain words ("my Rust target folders use 80 GB across git worktrees"). Talira searches the catalog using vector embeddings and uses Jev for filtering and reranking.

To try it:

- Search on https://talira.ai

- Add the MCP server to Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http --scope user talira https://mcp.talira.ai/mcp

Your agent can also send a report after each search: the problem in general terms, what you tried, what you kept and why. The idea is that it can eventually become a crowd-sourced database of tools that people actually chose and continued using over time.

It's currently in beta and the catalog still has a lot of gaps. I should also mention that I'm aware that ChatGPT and Claude already know a lot and are already very good at search. So there are plenty of cases where you don't need Talira at all. I'll need to collect some more real-world searches before I can benchmark it properly to see if it makes any difference.

I'd like to know if you've ever had any similar experiences. Let me know if an AI wasn't able to find a good solution that already existed.

Thanks for reading!

title.value: Show HN: Talira – Search engine for software, built for AI agents

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Fengli, founder of Inxpanse. HeyCube is our first product: the personalized feed for your always-on AI agents.

While building my own always-on agents, I kept watching the token and search API costs add up really fast. Then I noticed the scheduled tasks in ChatGPT/Grok Bot/etc. also use up a lot of your plan's allowance, often on checks that find nothing new. That's why many people still don't leave their agents truly always on.

This reminded me of the eras we humans have been through too: first search engines, then feeds. So I thought, why not build agents a feed of their own? That's why we built HeyCube. It reads sources around the clock and sends what fits you to the right agent, so your tokens go to the work itself. It's free and live at heycube.ai now, and works with ChatGPT, Grok Bot, Muse, Claude Code, and other agents in beta.

I'm looking forward to you giving your agents a feed and seeing what they can do. Let me know if you have any questions/comments/feature requests :) Thanks!

title.value: Show HN: HeyCube – The personalized feed for your always-on AI agents

story_text.value:
Pintura is designed for AI agents to work on plaintext files and for humans to review in a browser.

The premise is that when you're doing slides with AI agents, you mainly need to review their work and iterate until you're happy.

The main benefits are: 1. You can use git for version control and clear diffs. 2. The browser UI is designed for review: flip between versions with visual changes highlighted, pin comments, or drag/reword directly. 3. Your agent gets a CLI that helps it catch things like text overflow, misaligned elements, hanging words, etc.

It pairs with our spreadsheet companion Libreta (github.com/editide/libreta) if you want to link numbers. Clicking a linked number on a slide pops up a spreadsheet showing the formula or a screenshot of the original source.

I've been using this to build financial decks from the terminal with Claude Code (and now Antigravity). It's much nicer than flipping back and forth between Excel and PowerPoint. Here are some decks I've built with this setup: https://iterativaresearch.com/

Everything (preview, checks, screenshots, HTML/PDF export) is Apache-2.0 and runs locally with no account. PowerPoint export currently runs through our API with a free plan.

title.value: Show HN: Pintura – YAML Slides for agents to edit and humans to review
